candidate.educational_objective: Separate contemporaneous clinical documentation in the health record from organizational patient-safety event reporting.

options.A: Enter only the safety-event report because the reporting system replaces the need to document the client's assessment, injury, treatment, and notifications in the health record.
options.B: Document that an incident report was filed but omit the clinical details from the health record, because those details belong exclusively in the safety-event system.
options.C: Document the clinical facts, assessment, interventions, and notifications in the health record and submit a separate safety-event report according to facility policy.
options.D: Wait until risk management reviews the event before documenting it anywhere, because early documentation could conflict with the organization's later investigation.

candidate.rationale: Clinical care must be documented in the health record, while patient-safety event reporting serves a separate systems-learning function. AHRQ describes event reporting systems as mechanisms for capturing incidents, errors, near misses, and unsafe conditions so organizations can analyze hazards. The nurse should not substitute a safety-event report for contemporaneous clinical documentation.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Clinical facts and care belong in the health record, while the patient-safety event is also reported through the separate organizational event-reporting system.
candidate.source_locator: Incident reporting — event reports support organizational safety learning and do not replace contemporaneous documentation of the patient's condition and care in the health record
candidate.source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
